explanations.explanation: Right in the first verse: "You restored Jacob from captivity." Here Jacob stands for God's people. The sons of Korah, who wrote this song, open by remembering what the LORD already did. Good news like that is worth telling twice.

A new name is a nice gift, friend, but this verse doesn't mention one. It says the LORD showed favor to His land and "You restored Jacob from captivity." Jacob is the name of His people here. The song is about getting brought back, not about getting renamed.

No king shows up in this verse, baker. The sons of Korah say the LORD showed favor to His land and "You restored Jacob from captivity." Nobody gets crowned here. The favor is that His people were brought back from captivity.

That's it, friend: "You forgave the iniquity of Your people…" Iniquity is a heavy word, and the verse puts forgiveness right beside it. The singers put it right in the song. Then comes the word Selah, which I take as a spot to pause and let it sink in.

explanations.answer: He kept a record of it
explanations.explanation: Keeping a list is what we do with grudges, friend, and this verse says no such thing about the LORD. It says, "You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin." Forgiving and covering are what the sons of Korah remember. No ledger anywhere in the verse.

That's not what the singers remember. They say, "You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin." And the next verse says He withheld all His fury. Forgiveness is what they sing about here.

Close, but the singers say more than that. Verse 3 says, "You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger." The word is all, not part. Watch for that little word, because it carries the whole line.
Right, baker. The text says, "You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger." Not a little of it, not most of it. All of it. One tiny word, and it changes the whole line.

Yes, friend. They pray, "Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us." They call Him the God of their salvation, and then they ask. I think it takes real trust to ask that plainly.

Idols aren't in this prayer, baker. The sons of Korah ask God to restore them and to "…put away Your displeasure toward us." It's a short, plain request, and it's about God's displeasure toward them. The verse doesn't mention any idols.

No armies are mentioned in this prayer. The sons of Korah say, "Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us." There's no enemy in sight here. What they ask God to put away is His displeasure.

Yes, they really ask it: "Will You be angry with us forever?" The next question is just as bold: "Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?" Straight to Him, no tiptoeing. The song has room for the honest question.

They do ask it, friend. Verse 5 says, "Will You be angry with us forever?" Then they follow up with, "Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?" Two questions, one right after the other, and both of them are bold.

That's the word. "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" The revival has a purpose in the song: rejoicing in Him. I think a revived people with nothing to rejoice about would be like a fresh batch with no chocolate chips, and nobody wants that batch.

Mourning isn't in this line, friend. The prayer says, "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" Rejoice is the word the singers chose. They're asking to be brought back to life so they can celebrate Him.

Settling down sounds peaceful, baker, but it's not the word here. The verse asks, "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" Rejoice is a bigger word than settle. They're asking to be brought back to life so they can celebrate Him.

explanations.answer: Listen to what God will say
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" He did all that asking, and now he says he will listen. A lot of us ask and then start talking again before anybody answers. This singer says he's going to listen.

explanations.answer: Go up to the house of God
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse sends him to the house of God. The singer says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" The verse leaves out where he is or where he goes. It only says what he'll do: listen.

explanations.answer: Write the prayer on a scroll
explanations.explanation: The singer doesn't mention a scroll in this verse, friend. He says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" The song keeps it simple. After all the asking, he says he will listen.
That's the one. The singer says, "…He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints…" Surely, he says. He's not guessing. He's sure of what God will speak.
The word isn't judgment, baker. The singer says, "…He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints…" Surely is a confident word. What he's sure of is peace.

No warnings in this line, friend. The text says, "…He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints…" And the verse goes on to say that He will not let them return to folly. Peace is what the singer expects to hear.
It's the opposite, baker. The verse says, "He will not let them return to folly." That's a promise the singer is sure of. It comes right after the part about God speaking peace.
Right, friend. The singer says, "He will not let them return to folly." That's the end of verse 8, and it sits right beside God speaking peace. The singer sounds sure of both.
Yes, baker: "Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him…" Near is a good word. It's not far off, and it's not a rumor. The singer says it with confidence.

The singer says the opposite, friend. Verse 9 says, "Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him…" Near means close, and the singer opens with surely, so he isn't hedging. I'd say that's a man who has already made up his mind about how close God is.
Yes, baker: "righteousness and peace have kissed." It's a picture, and a sweet one. Two things you might expect to be strangers meet like old friends. I love that the singer chose such a warm image.

The picture goes the other way, friend. The verse says, "Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed." Everything in that line is coming together. Nobody is walking away.

No fighting in this picture, baker. Verse 10 says, "Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed." It's a gentle line, and it's all about coming together. Fists aren't part of it.
Yes, earth: "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth…" It comes up like a little green shoot out of the ground. And the very next piece of the picture comes from the other direction, from heaven.

That's the one: "…righteousness looks down from heaven." So the picture has one thing coming up from the earth and another looking down from above. Faithfulness sprouts from below, righteousness looks down from above, and both are in the same verse.

No sea in this verse, friend. The singer says, "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven." The two places he names are earth and heaven. The sea never makes the list.

Mountains are a fine guess, baker, but the singer picked other spots. He says, "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven." One comes up and one looks down. That's a whole picture, and it didn't need a single mountain.

Zion doesn't show up anywhere in this psalm, friend. Verse 11 says, "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven." The earth and heaven are the two places in this picture. No city is named.

Yes, baker: "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase." Indeed is the singer planting his flag. He isn't saying the LORD might provide good. He's saying it will happen, and I'd put that on a cookie box.

No king in this verse, friend. The singer says, "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase." What He provides is good, and the land yields its increase. The verse doesn't say what that good looks like.

A city wall is a fine thing, baker, but it didn't make this batch. The singer is looking at the land and what it yields. He says, "The LORD will indeed provide what is good…" Good and a harvest are what this verse hands us, and no bricks are on the list.

explanations.answer: To prepare the way for His steps
explanations.explanation: That's the last line of the song: "Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps." Righteousness goes first and gets the road ready. I think it's a lovely way to close. Right where the psalm ends, it points to Him walking.

explanations.answer: To clear the nations from the land
explanations.explanation: No nations get cleared in this verse. The singer says, "Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps." Righteousness goes ahead of Him, and the reason is to prepare the way. It's a quiet picture, not a battle.

explanations.answer: To guard the gates of His city
explanations.explanation: No gates or guards in this verse, friend. It says, "Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps." Righteousness walks ahead and prepares the way. The singer doesn't mention a city.
